notes: Customer quote: 'We need predictable tail latency for live support—cannot have 99th spikes during peak business hours.'
Primary constraint: latency SLO alignment across stack (client SDK timing, network, ingress, model runtime).
They prefer p50/p95/p99 split for routing: p50 used for UX snappiness; p95 for UX budgets; p99 used for incident thresholds and escalation.

Streaming vs non-streaming: want separate SLOs. Streaming (token-by-token) measured as time-to-first-token (TT1) and time-to-last-token (TTLast) for long responses. Non-streaming measured as time-to-complete response. Need clarity on which percentile maps to which metric.
Measurement alignment asks (from SE workshop):
- Define client-side timing (end-to-end) vs server-only (ingress->egress).
- Agree on excluded events: cold starts, provisioning windows, scheduled maintenance windows, first-request-after-deploy warmups.
- Percentile computation: use global aggregation over rolling 30d for billing SLAs; use rolling 7d for operational alerts. Clarify whether per-route percentiles or global product percentiles.
Suggested SLOs (working draft):
- Chat non-streaming: p50 < 80ms, p95 < 220ms, p99 < 420ms (client-side, excluding cold starts),
- Chat streaming: TT1 p50 < 60ms, TT1 p95 < 180ms, TTLast p95 < 600ms (server-side + network),
- Embeddings vectorize: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 90ms, p99 < 200ms (per-text request),
- Reranking batch: median per-request depends on batch size; target p95 < 250ms for typical batch sizes used in POC.
Important notes on measurement methodology:

- Client SDK will emit client-side timestamps (request_started, first_byte, complete) and attach request_id. Redwood will correlate server-side timestamps for ingress and egress and return aligned timing in Console logs.
- Need deterministic clock alignment guidance: prefer using monotonic SDK timers and server-provided clock offset correction. Discuss NTP drift handling for on-prem gateways.
- Sampling strategy: 100% synthetic testing + 1% production real-user traces with PII-safe redaction for SLO validation. Traces retained for 90 days for investigation.
POC measurement plan specifics:
- Synthetic runner: colocated in same VPC to measure lower-bound network latency; separate runner outside VPC to measure customer internet variance.
- Load profile: 300 RPS steady + 3x hourly spikes to simulate peak; run for 72-hour window to capture diurnal patterns.
- Reserved GPU planning: initial POC pool 4xA100 equiv (NVIDIA A100 80GB quantized workload profile). If p95 targets miss, escalate to 8-node pool or enable burst autoscale policy.
- Batching/kv-cache impact: SE explained tradeoff — larger batch sizes reduce cost but increase tail; they want conservative batch cap for chat SLOs.
SLA negotiation points to resolve:

- Definition of violation (client-side vs server-side percentiles). Customer insists on client-side for commercial SLA; Redwood prefers server-side for operational measurability. Need middle ground: commercial SLA measured server-side + allowance for network delta (e.g., +50ms).
- Remedies: credit thresholds at p99 breach sustained >1 hour across region. Customer asked for automatic fallback to smaller model variant under heavy load.
Open technical risks:
- On-prem gateway clock skew complicates percentiles if client timestamps used—require sync guidance or server-side canonical timing.
- Quantization/model variant fallbacks may change per-token costs and latency characteristics; need baseline benchmark per model variant for inclusion in SLO.
- Streaming measurements can be noisy for long continuations; propose measuring TT1 and median token inter-arrival time separately.
